catalog_snapshot.label: Aggregator-shadow presence only
catalog_snapshot.definition: The business's entire indexed footprint consists of auto-generated directory mirrors (loc8nearme, sagemenu, wanderlog, novacircle, timetoopen) that republish stale or wrong fields — no claimed platform profile, no owned site. Discovery fails two ways: the mirrors disagree with each other (name, category, hours), and search engines surface the mirror instead of the business, so nothing authoritative exists to click through to. Observed this pass: Babushka/Best International Foods exists almost entirely as mirror pages; novacircle mislabels Tala Euro-Russian Mart as a 'restaurant'.

catalog_snapshot.label: Rename residue splits the discovery trace
catalog_snapshot.definition: When an ethnic grocery changes hands or rebrands, directories, certification registries and mirrors keep indexing the predecessor name while the live storefront trades under a new one. Searchers for the current name surface stale predecessor-name mirrors; searches for the old name hit a live-looking but dead record. Review equity, hours and category signals never consolidate on the current identity, and address-keyed joins split the same storefront into two thin half-entities. Milwaukee this pass showed three independent chains: Noor Supermarket to Rayan Market (4563 S 13th, same phone), Sasta Bazaar to Raja Bazaar (709 W Mitchell), Al-Asalah to Samah (851 W Layton).
signals: two names share one address and phone where one is a predecessor, not a concurrent alias
mirror pages carry the dead name with current-looking hours/reviews while the live name has a thin profile
the business's own page or community records acknowledge the rename ('Previously X')
directory slugs preserve the dead name inside URLs that surface for the new name (loc8nearme's Rayan page lives at /noor-meat-and-grocery-store/)
expected_vectors: rename-chain detection (same address+phone, different name across directories)
mirror-vs-canonical name diff audit per address

catalog_snapshot.label: Fractional-unit address breaks NAP consolidation
catalog_snapshot.definition: Storefronts addressed with fractional units (e.g. '3009 1/2 Independence Ave') fail address normalization across maps, license registries, and directories: the fractional variant, the bare street number, and neighboring suite numbers are treated as different places, so the same operating storefront accumulates several thin half-profiles instead of one consolidated listing. Reviews, hours, and category signals never pool on a single surface, so none of the fragments ranks, and address-keyed cross-joins (license ↔ platform) silently miss the business. Observed in Kansas City: Al-Hallal Grocery Store at 3009 1/2 Independence Ave trades under a license chain (Tawakal Halal Store Inc → Al-Hallal LLC → Darsalaam Grocery Store LLC) while community listings split the same storefront across name and address variants.

license/registry address differs from directory addresses only by the fractional suffix

expected_vectors: fractional-address variant cross-join between license registries and platform listings
address-normalization sweep (fractional/suite/½ variants) per commercial corridor
identity-conflict detection keyed on phone + normalized parcel

suggested_reasons.proposed_label: Bank community-reinvestment feature is the only current trace
suggested_reasons.proposed_definition: A local bank or credit union publishes a community-feature post (community reinvestment / "Love" campaign) naming the storefront and its neighborhood impact, and that editorial post becomes the business's most recent indexed public signal. The post ranks for the business name, but it carries no NAP, no hours, and no category field, so category-filtered and map-based discovery never resolves the storefront from it; the operator controls none of the content. The blind spot is a discovery mechanic (the only fresh trace lives in an unrelated financial-institution channel), not a business attribute.
observed_signals: most recent indexed mention of the business is a bank/credit-union community or reinvestment post
the post names the business and neighborhood but carries no address, hours, or category
no corresponding first-party or claimed-platform surface exists

suggested_reasons.proposed_label: Principal-office address splits from storefront address
suggested_reasons.proposed_definition: The entity's registered principal office (or benefit-program registration) address differs from the operating storefront address. Directories and mirrors ingest the regulatory address and publish a listing at a location that is not the walk-in store, while the storefront address carries only a thin or generic listing. Address-keyed joins then treat one operating business as two weak entities, and a searcher who finds the regulatory address is routed to a non-retail location. Distinct from a rename (the name is stable) and from fractional-unit normalization (both addresses are well-formed) — the failure is the registry-vs-storefront split itself.

one address resolves to a non-retail principal office (suite/office park) and the other to a walk-in retail unit
same phone or entity id ties the two addresses together

prohibited_inferences: Low digital quality describes observable online fields only — never infer low revenue, low customer volume, poor products, poor service, or sales readiness from a thin digital footprint.
A bronze slot is not a prospect verdict and not a competitive benchmark; these businesses are not framed as outreach targets or compared to high-visibility competitors.
An empty slot never means no such business exists — it means the vectors executed did not reach one (or were not executed).

A filled absent_from_platform or field-gap slot is a per-platform finding — a business absent on Google may be fully present on Yelp; a per-platform gap is never generalized into a whole-business verdict.
Bronze output is a discovery-calibration artifact and must never be framed as competitive benchmarking.
